## Understanding the problem

We may change **at most one** character of `s` to any letter, then ask whether the resulting string is a subsequence of `t`. A replacement does not delete anything — the modified string still has length `len(s)`, so all `m` characters must be matched to `m` distinct, order-preserving indices of `t`.

**Example 1:** `s = "cat"`, `t = "chat"`. Here `s` is *already* a subsequence of `t` (`c@0, a@2, t@3`), so the answer is immediately `true` — the replacement is optional.

**Example 2:** `s = "plane"`, `t = "apple"`. Even ignoring one character of `s`, the leftovers cannot line up: after matching `p`, `l`, `e` there is no way to place the other two characters in order, and no single swap fixes this, so the answer is `false`.

With lengths up to $10^5$, anything like $O(m \cdot n)$ per test is risky, and trying all 26 letters per position is far too slow. We need linear-time preprocessing.
k: Replacing s[p] means: match s[0..p-1] against a prefix of t, reserve one free index of t for the replaced letter, then match s[p+1..m-1] against a suffix of t.

Greedy left-to-right matching gives, for every prefix length, the minimum number of t-characters needed (pre[]); greedy right-to-left matching gives, for every suffix, the maximum starting index in t (suf[]).
A replacement at position p works exactly when pre[p] < suf[p+1] — there is at least one unclaimed index of t between the two matched parts.
If s is already a subsequence of t, position p = 0 always satisfies the condition, so the zero-replacement case falls out naturally.

a.n: Approach 1: Try Every Split Point with Fresh Scans (Brute Force)
a.i: For each candidate replacement index `p`, independently verify with two pointers that `s[0..p-1]` matches a prefix of `t` and that `s[p+1..m-1]` matches a suffix of `t` leaving at least one index (the one right after the prefix) free for the replaced letter. This is the direct translation of the definition and needs no preprocessing, but rescanning `t` for every `p` costs $O(m \cdot n)$ in the worst case — acceptable only for tiny inputs, included here to build intuition.
s: For each p from 0 to m-1:
Scan t left to right matching s[0..p-1]; let j be the first unused index after the match (fail p if the prefix doesn't fit).
Scan t right to left matching s[p+1..m-1], never touching indices <= j (index j is reserved for the replaced character); fail p if the suffix doesn't fit.
If both parts fit for any p, return true; otherwise return false.
a.t: O(m · n) — for each of m split points we rescan t twice.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — only pointers and flags.

a.i: Compute once, for every i, `pre[i]` = the minimum number of leading characters of `t` needed to greedily match `s[0..i-1]` (infinity if impossible), and `suf[i]` = the maximum index in `t` at which `s[i..m-1]` can greedily match (-1 if impossible). Replacing index `p` succeeds iff `pre[p] < suf[p+1]`: the prefix occupies indices `[0, pre[p])`, the replaced letter can take index `pre[p]`, and the suffix occupies `[suf[p+1], n)`. Greedy minimality/maximality guarantees that if any valid assignment of indices exists, these extreme values expose it. One extra check `pre[m] <= n` covers the zero-replacement case.
s: Build pre[] left to right with a two-pointer greedy subsequence match; mark unreachable prefixes with infinity (= n+1).
If pre[m] <= n, s is already a subsequence — return true.
Build suf[] right to left: suf[m] = n, and suf[i] is the largest k < suf[i+1] with t[k] == s[i], or -1.
Return true if any p in [0, m-1] satisfies pre[p] < suf[p+1]; otherwise false.
a.t: O(n + m) — each of the three passes advances its pointer monotonically over t or s.
a.sp: O(m) — the pre[] and suf[] arrays of length m+1.

## Wrap-up

In an interview, state the brute-force framing first (fix the replaced index, match prefix and suffix independently), then immediately optimize by observing that the prefix and suffix scans can be **precomputed** for all split points in one forward and one backward pass — landing on the $O(n+m)$ solution.

**Common pitfalls:**
- Forgetting that the replaced character still needs its own index in `t` (nothing is deleted), hence the strict inequality `pre[p] < suf[p+1]` rather than `<=`.
- Assuming a naive "skip on first mismatch" greedy works — it conflates skipping a `t` character with replacing an `s` character and is incorrect.
- Leaving stale zeros in `pre[]` after the greedy match fails early; unreachable prefixes must be marked infinite.
- Edge cases: `m > n` (always false, handled naturally), single-character strings, and `s` already a subsequence (answer true with no replacement).

**Follow-ups to expect:** generalize to *at most k* replacements (DP over positions with `dp[i][k]` = minimal t-index, solvable with per-layer two pointers), or return the actual replacement index/character instead of a boolean.
